title: Signature Chisel Sharpening
description: Signature design: A sharp chisel cuts with light pressure and leaves a clean surface, while a dull chisel needs force, slips, and crushes wood fibers. Sharpening a chisel means flattening the back first, then honing the bevel: the back must be flat so the cutting edge is a true intersection of two planes. Hone the primary bevel at about 25 degrees, then add a microbevel about 5 degrees steeper for a durable 30 degree cutting edge. Work through the grits without skipping, and test the edge by paring end grain: a sharp chisel leaves a smooth, shiny surface with little effort. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection, keep fingers behind the cutting edge, and move the tool away from the body on the stone. Never test sharpness by running a thumb across the edge.

title: Signature Plane Iron Sharpening
description: Signature design: A plane iron is sharpened like a chisel, but its edge must be straight and square across its width, or the plane will cut steps into the surface. Flatten the back, hone the bevel at about 30 degrees, and check the edge against a square after each grit: a skewed edge planes a skewed surface. A slight camber, a barely curved edge, suits smoothing planes because the corners do not dig in, but a jack plane iron can carry more camber for heavy removal. After honing, set the iron in the plane with a fine mouth opening and a thin shaving, then test on a board edge. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Hand Saw Sharpening Basics
description: Signature design: Sharpening a hand saw means filing each tooth to a point with consistent size, set, and angle, and it is the most skill-demanding sharpening in this guide. Joint the teeth first by running a flat file over them so every tooth is the same height, then file each tooth with a triangular file sized to the tooth, keeping the file level and at the tooth's rake angle. Set, the sideways bend of alternate teeth, makes the kerf wider than the blade so the saw does not bind; too much set makes a rough, wandering cut. Beginners should practice on an old saw before filing a good one. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Knife Honing
description: Signature design: Honing a knife realigns the fine edge that folds over in use, and it is maintenance, not grinding: a honing steel or a fine stone straightens the edge without removing much metal. Hold the knife at its edge angle, about 15 degrees per side for a kitchen knife with a 5 degree microbevel addition for a 20 degree total, and draw the edge along the steel from heel to tip in smooth strokes, alternating sides. A knife that still drags after honing needs true sharpening on stones, because honing cannot restore an edge that is chipped or rounded. Test by slicing paper: a honed knife cuts cleanly without tearing. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Drill Bit Sharpening
description: Signature design: A drill bit is sharpened by grinding its two cutting lips to equal length and angle, with a standard point angle of 118 degrees for general work. Unequal lips make the bit drill oversize holes and wander, because the longer lip does all the cutting. Grind each lip against the wheel with the bit held at half the point angle to the wheel face, cool the bit in water often so the steel does not overheat and lose temper, and check both lips with a gauge. A correctly sharpened bit cuts with two even spirals of waste and needs only light feed pressure. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Router Bit Care
description: Signature design: Router bits cut with carbide edges that stay sharp a long time but chip if abused, and care means cleaning, inspection, and correct handling rather than frequent grinding. Clean pitch and resin from bits with a resin remover and a brass brush, never a steel brush that can nick carbide, and inspect the edges under light: a chipped edge leaves a ridged cut and must be professionally sharpened or replaced. Store bits in their case or a rack where edges cannot knock together, and always check that the collet grips the shank fully, at least 3/4 inch of shank inside the collet, before switching the router on. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Tool Rust Removal
description: Signature design: Rust removal restores a tool without grinding away good steel: start with the gentlest method that works and step up only as needed. Light rust comes off with a Scotch-Brite pad and oil, moderate rust with fine wet-or-dry paper used with oil, and heavy rust with a vinegar soak followed by neutralizing, drying, and oiling, because vinegar left on steel invites new rust. Work through the grits 80, then 150, then 220, then 320 for a surface that can be protected, and always finish with oil or wax, because bare steel rusts again quickly in a damp shop. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Handle Repair and Replacement
description: Signature design: A loose or cracked handle makes a tool unsafe, because the head can fly off in use, so handle work is safety work. Remove a broken handle by drilling out the old wood and driving the remainder out from the eye, fit the new handle by shaping it to the eye and seating it with the grain running along the handle length, and secure it with a wedge driven across the grain plus a metal wedge if the tool maker specifies one. A handle blank 1-1/2 inches square and 12 inches long suits many small striking tools; shape it with a spokeshave and rasp, sand it smooth, and finish it with oil so it does not dry and shrink. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Tool Storage Systems
description: Signature design: A tool storage system keeps tools findable, protected, and dry, and the best system is the one that puts each tool back in the same place every time. Wall panels and French cleats suit hand tools, drawers with dividers suit small tools and bits, and cutting edges need guards or racks so they do not knock together. Plan the wall area first: a panel 48 inches wide by 24 inches high holds a useful hand-tool set, and every tool gets an outline or label so a missing tool is obvious at a glance. Keep the storage dry, because tools stored against a damp wall rust even in a closed shop. title: Signature Workbench Maintenance

title: Signature Saw Blade Cleaning
description: Signature design: A saw blade caked with pitch and resin cuts hotter, slower, and rougher than a clean blade, and cleaning restores it without any grinding. Remove the blade from the saw first, soak it briefly in a pitch remover or a warm detergent solution, and scrub the teeth and gullets with a brass brush, never a steel brush that can dull carbide tips. Rinse, dry the blade fully so it does not rust, and lightly oil the plate before storing or refitting it. A 10 inch blade, 254 millimeters across, is the common table-saw size, and its teeth must be counted and inspected while it is out: a missing or chipped tooth means professional service. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Plane Tuning
description: Signature design: Tuning a plane means setting its parts so it cuts thin, even shavings: the iron sharp, the chipbreaker close to the edge, the mouth fine, and the sole flat. Set the chipbreaker about 1/32 inch behind the cutting edge for fine work, close the mouth so the shaving thickness nearly fills it, and check the sole with a straightedge, lapping it flat if it rocks. A mouth opening of 0.003 inch with a shaving of 0.002 inch leaves only 0.001 inch of clearance, which is the fine setting a smoothing plane wants. Adjust one thing at a time and test after each change, or the cause of any improvement is lost. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Square Calibration Checks
description: Signature design: A square is only useful while it is true, so calibration checks belong in regular maintenance: draw a line against the square, flip it, and draw again, and the lines must coincide. For a large square, the 3-4-5 check is stronger: a triangle with sides 12, 16, and 20 inches must have a true right angle, and its diagonal must measure exactly 20 inches. A combination square can be adjusted by tapping or filing its stock, but a framing square that is out of true is usually replaced or professionally trued, because bending it risks a worse error. Record the check date on the tool so the next check is not forgotten. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Oil and Wax Tool Protection
description: Signature design: Oil and wax protect tool steel and wooden handles from moisture, and the rule is simple: clean the tool, apply a thin coat, and wipe it nearly dry, because a thick coat attracts dust and a missing coat invites rust. Camellia oil suits cutting edges, boiled linseed oil suits handles and bench tops, and paste wax suits cast-iron tables that must stay slick but rust-free. Apply to a surface 36 inches by 12 inches, for example a plane sole and sides, with a rag, let it sit briefly, then buff it dry. Reapply after any use in damp conditions and at least seasonally in a dry shop. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Workshop Tool Inventory
description: Signature design: A workshop tool inventory lists every tool, its condition, and its place, and it turns lost tools and duplicate purchases into rare events. Walk the shop with a notebook, record each tool and its storage place, note anything damaged or dull, and give each storage slot a label that matches the list. A shelf run 120 inches long with 6 inch end margins and 13 slots gives 9 inch spacing per slot, a practical layout for hand tools on a wall shelf. Review the inventory twice a year, update it when a tool is bought or retired, and keep a copy away from the shop in case of fire or theft. title: Signature Seasonal Tool Care
description: Signature design: Seasonal tool care is the twice-yearly pass that catches rust, dull edges, and dried handles before they become damage: clean every tool, sharpen what is dull, oil what is bare, and check handles and cords. Work through the grits 220, then 320, then 400, then 600 on surfaces that need refinishing, always ascending, and never jump from coarse to fine without the steps between, or deep scratches survive under a shiny finish. In damp seasons, add a wax coat to cast iron and check the shop for leaks, and in dry seasons, oil wooden handles so they do not shrink and loosen. Record the pass date so the next one is not missed. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.
